newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori, evoking 1980s chaos, vows to resist MRTA.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori, evoking 1980s chaos, vows to resist MRTA.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's house have grabbed world headlines but will not succeed in pushing Peru back into the chaos of the past, President Alberto Fujimori said on Wednesday.

Speaking at a conference of Central Bank officials from the Americas and Spain, he said Peru had regained peace and stability after "practically collapsing" under the weight of leftist guerrilla violence and economic crises in the 1980s.
"We had inflation of 7,000 percent and uncontrollable violence at the hands of terrorism. Our credibility was in shambles," said Fujimori, who took office when Peru's economy hit bottom in 1990.

Trying to quell international fears of a new spiral of violence, he said Peru was not going to be destabilised by the 113-day standoff with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) in an affluent Lima suburb.

"In spite of the incident at the Japanese ambassador's residence, which has made news around the world, Peru's stability can be seen both in the economy and on the streets," he said. "It's a stability and reconstruction ... strong enough to stand up to shifts and impasses."

About 20 MRTA fighters swept into the ambassador's home in Lima during a cocktail party on Dec. 17 and took the guests hostage to demand freedom for about 450 jailed comrades. They gradually released all but 72 of their captives, keeping a VIP list including Fujimori's brother Pedro, two Cabinet ministers and the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia.

A three-man mediation panel, made up of Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, Vatican representative Juan Luis Cipriani and Red Cross official Michel Minnig, entered the besieged home on Wednesday for new talks with the MRTA. They spent nearly three hours inside and had no comment later.
A key ally of Fujimori, Congress president Victor Joy Way, urged patience in talks to end the siege, saying the government would win less favourable terms if it rushed to an agreement.
"Our enemy is not time," Joy Way told reporters while on a visit to Shanghai. "The key element is patience. The first to lose patience will have less opportunity for a solution."

Fujimori has been under strong pressure from Tokyo to speed negotiations to free the hostages, who include about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats. But face-to-face talks between the government and MRTA have been on hold for nearly a month, deadlocked over the guerrillas' demand for freedom for their jailed comrades.

The Japanese "are being very demanding," a government source close to Fujimori said. "Obviously there is great pressure from them but we have told them we are not going to cave in. We will not free the MRTA prisoners."

The source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said he believed Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was under domestic political pressure to get the hostages freed soon but "the (Peruvian) government's strategy is to wait."

Nonetheless, he said, indirect talks through a three-man mediation team had yielded progress. "There are advances. I think this could end in a relatively short time. It could end sooner than people think."
